WRT Summary Description of and Rationale for Proposed Changes to Program Name Change The Department of Writing and Rhetoric’s name does not accurately and fully reflect the research work, course and degree offerings, and trajectory of the department, nor does it resonate with students.
A more representative name for the department is the “Department of Professional and Public Writing.” Furthermore, with national trends favoring professional and technical writing careers, it is imperative that students (current and prospective) and colleagues are aware of our talent and specialty in this area.
This name change is expected to help us recruit students, promote research collaborations (both within and outside the institution), develop online graduate certificate programs, and attract new hires in professional and technical communication.
We anticipate a growing need for departments with this specialization.
The U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment in technical writing occupations to grow 12 percent from 2020 to 2030, which is faster than the average for all occupations.
It documents the median wage for technical writers as $74,650.

As a faculty, we are well positioned for this change.
WRT faculty hold doctorates in Professional and Technical Writing and are nationally recognized, award-winning researchers in the field.
Areas of expertise include, but are not limited to, technical communication, procedural discourse, user-experience design, civic and community literacy, digital and multimodal writing, cultural rhetorics, information design, accessibility, and science communication.
The department course offerings already reflect this expertise.
The department faculty officially voted to change the department name to the “Department of Professional and Public Writing” on November 22, 2021.
Concentration Areas We are proposing two areas of concentration that capitalize on our strengths as a department and that track with career pathways, at the same time that they fulfill our goal of encouraging civic engagement: Technical Writing and Professional and Civic Writing.
Students may select three courses to fulfill a concentration area.
Note that none of the concentration areas includes the revised core courses (see below).

Consistent with College strategic plans, concentrations will provide students in the major with an opportunity to customize the major in a way that more effectively coheres with specific career objectives.
Lastly, a nine-credit or three-course sequence constitutes a concentration that will be noted on students’ transcripts.
Revised Core Requirements We are proposing new core requirements in keeping with the latest research in Writing Studies, research into student needs, the Agenda for Change, and the Academic Strategic Plan.
The proposed core reduces the number of requirements to give majors a chance to embark on courses of study best suited to their interests and career paths.
The new requirements represent vertical integration of some of the most exciting and forward-focused of our courses.
In this core, students will find an introduction to the major, an introduction to digital writing, and a capstone that will send students into the world with a professional portfolio.
Moreover, it contains courses that emphasize the Agenda for Change.

We are retiring courses that, in their current form, are considered outdated and Eurocentric by current scholars and pedagogues in the field (201* and 360).
Instead we will integrate the aspects of these courses that are still useful and relevant into the new core courses.
The new core will contain the following courses: WRT 104: Writing to Inform and Explain.
This course is our flagship first-year writing course that offers some of the most innovative pedagogy available at the university level.
The course offers an introduction to many of the advanced courses in the major.
In particular, it introduces students to digital writing, later reinforced in other courses.
It also forwards the Agenda for Change by promoting a learner-centered classroom in which all students— regardless of preparation—can succeed.
This course also forms part of the Harrington core.
WRT 235: Digital Writing and Rhetoric.
In 235, writers practice the craft of digital writing using a wide array of contemporary digital tools and multiple modes including text, images, videos, and sound, as well as spatial and gestural modes.
We introduce the theory of digital writing and support production by assigning complex digital

genres for diverse digital audiences. This newly revised course also reinforces rhetorical theory and argument in more relevant and culturally inclusive ways. WRT 371G: Write Now: Race, Resistance, and Language Justice. Language is central to racial and cultural identity. Through interdisciplinary perspectives, this course prompts students to consider how language shapes understandings of race and identity and how they can use it as a means to pursue social justice. This course (provisionally approved by the Faculty Senate) speaks directly to the University’s Action Agenda. WRT 495: Advanced Digital Writing and Rhetoric. In this capstone course, students apply cumulative knowledge to create a professional digital portfolio that they can use to secure the career of their choice. In 495, students learn advanced digital writing and rhetorical theory, as well as advanced production skills. *Note: The Public Relations, Data Science, and Computer Science programs currently list 201 as a possible elective in their core. We have spoken with the chairs/directors of these departments, and all support its removal from our course offerings. All three program leaders believe that WRT 235 or 227 would be more relevant to their majors. Program Prerequisites Admission to this program requires a Bachelors degree in Computer Science, Statistics, Biostatistics, Mathematics, Engineering, or a closely related field.
A Master’s degree is encouraged but not required.
Common requirements include course work covering the material in the following courses: • MTH 141 – Calculus 1 • MTH 142 – Calculus 2 • MTH 215 – Introduction to Linear Algebra • One course in Mathematics or Statistics for which calculus is a prerequisite All applicants will need to take the GRE.
In addition, international applicants will need to report their TOEFL scores.
Waivers can be granted at the discretion of the graduate director.
GRE subject in Mathematics or Computer Science are not required but can be favorably assessed by the admission committee.

Specific Prerequisites for Computer Science Concentration In addition to the general requirements applicants with a bachelors degree in an unrelated field will be considered provided they have completed course work covering the material in • CSC 211 Object-Oriented Programming • CSC 212 Data Structures and Abstractions • CSC 301 Fundamentals of Programming Languages • CSC 340: Applied Combinatorics • CSC 440 Design and Analysis of Algorithms Specific Prerequisites for Statistics Concentration In addition to the general requirements, following courses or their equivalents (will need approval of the graduate program chair) may be required to be admitted to our program if a student lacks a strong quantitative background.
However, these requirements may be waived based on prior experience in industry or research.

• MTH 243 – Calculus for Functions of Several Variables • STA 409 – Statistical Methods in Research I • STA 412 – Statistical Methods in Research II • MTH 451 – Intro Probability and Statistics • MTH 452 - Mathematical Statistics Ph.D.
Program Requirements The student must complete a total of at least 72 academic credits beyond the bachelors degree as follows: • At least 52 credits in coursework or 14 classes (3 or 4 credits each) • At least 18 dissertation research credits • At least 2 credit hours in seminar series (1 credit hour per semester).
Attendance strongly encouraged for all full time students.
A student entering the program with an M.S. degree in Computer Science, Statistics or a related area may be granted up to 30 credits toward the Ph.D. in Computer and Statistical Sciences.
A program of study can include at most three courses at the 400-level.
Students who have undergraduate credits for a particular 400-level course (or equivalent) cannot repeat the course for graduate credit.

Specific Requirements for Computer Science Concentration Students must complete: • Four graduate CSC courses decided after consulting the graduate committee. • Four more CSC courses or equivalent approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • At least one graduate STA course approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • Other courses must be selected in order to meet the coursework minimum and will be selected in consultation with the student’s advisor or major professor.
Specific Requirements for Statistics Concentration Students must complete: • Five graduate STA courses decided after consulting the graduate committee. • Four more graduate statistics courses approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • At least one CSC graduate course approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • Other courses must be selected in order to meet the coursework minimum and will be selected in consultation with the student’s advisor or major professor.

Milestone 1: Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination will consist of written exams, with the purpose of testing the student’s knowledge of specific core areas for their concentration of studies. A waiver could be granted to a student from taking an exam in one of the areas where the student can demonstrate competence in that area. Waivers could be granted at the time of admission. The qualifying examination should be taken within the first 30 program credits. Core areas for Computer Science Concentration Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination requirements cover the material of CSC 301, 340, 411, 412, 440, and 445. These requirements are checked at the time of admission Core areas for Statistics Concentration Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination requirements cover the material of MTH 451 and 452, STA 502, 542, and 545. These requirements are checked at the time of admission. Milestone 2: Comprehensive Exam Students must take a comprehensive examination, which is composed of a written examination and an oral examination. Typically, a student would be expected to take the comprehensive examination within two years after joining the program. A candidate whose comprehensive exam performance is deemed as failing by the Graduate Committee may, with the recommendation of the committee and the approval of the Graduate School, be permitted one re-examination, to be taken no sooner than four months and no later than one year after the initial examination. Milestone 3: Dissertation Defense Students are expected to write a Ph.D. dissertation, under the supervision of a Major Professor and a graduate committee, according to the rules established by the Graduate School.
